newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-GRAF SAYS HELPING IN APPEARANCE MONEY PROBE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF SAYS HELPING IN APPEARANCE MONEY PROBE.

text.p: World number one Steffi Graf confirmed on Friday that the professional women's tennis circuit was investigating claims she took appearance money against the tour's rules.
Graf, who risks a three month ban if the allegations are proved, told reporters after a third-round victory at the Australian Open on Friday she was cooperating with the probe.
"That's correct. That's been going on for a few months," the top seed and multi-millionaire said when asked about the investigation. "The WTA is working on that and I'm helping them as best I can."

Graf declined to comment on the substance of the allegations, raised at the trial of her father, Peter Graf, on charges he evaded over US$12 million in tax on the player's earnings between 1989 and 1993.

Peter Graf spent over a year in a German prison awaiting trial. The verdict is expected to be handed down shortly before the Australian Open women's singles final on January 25 -- and Graf has said she will play on whatever happens.
On the tennis court, Graf has barely faltered despite her father's legal problems.
She has won all six of her last grand slam tournaments and is favourite here to add a fifth Australian Open title to her staggering career record of 21 grand slam victories.

Peter Graf's trial has heard the German Tennis Federation (DTB) admit it paid his daughter hundreds of thousands of dollars annually for "services and advertising" in connection with DTB-run events in Hamburg and Berlin.
DTB chief Guenter Sanders said the cash, said to be between $150,000 and $270,000 a year between 1990 and 1993, was paid to ensure the tournaments had a big-name attraction.
Under the rules of the WTA, which runs the women's tour, players who accept appearance money are liable to a fine of up to $50,000 and a 90-day ban.
German public prosecutors involved in Peter Graf's much-publicised tax trial said on Wednesday the WTA had contacted their office for details of the alleged payments.
"A lawyer representing the WTA in Germany has contacted us by phone but we demand requests in writing and we have not had that," Mannheim public prosecutor Hubert Jobski said.
"We will have to look at any request and check it carefully. There are German laws on tax secrecy."

Graf, who has said the tennis court is her "holiday" from mounting off-court pressures, showed minor vulnerability in her third-round match against Argentine Ines Gorrochategui, coming back from 1-4 in the opening set to take the match 7-5 6-3.
"I didn't move very well from the beginning," said Graf, who still feels the lingering effects of a back injury which forced her retire in the final of the Philadelphia event in November.
"I just need to focus a bit better," she added.
Graf next meets South African 12th seed Amanda Coetzer in the fourth round.
